Where it began

Daniel Vettori was born in Auckland on 27 January 1979 and grew up in Hamilton, where he went to St Paul's Collegiate School. He began as a medium-pacer before turning to left-arm spin, the craft that would make his name.

He first played for Northern Districts in 1996–97, and within months he was in the Test side. He made his debut against England in February 1997, aged 18, which made him New Zealand's youngest Test cricketer up to then. He was the 200th player to earn a New Zealand Test cap. A few weeks later he took his first five-wicket haul, against Sri Lanka.

The player

Vettori played 113 Tests between 1997 and 2014. He took 362 wickets at 34.37, with 20 five-wicket innings and three ten-wicket matches, and made 4,531 runs at 30.01 with six hundreds. He was the youngest man up to then to reach 100 Test wickets, doing it by the age of 21, and in 2009 he became only the second New Zealander, after Richard Hadlee, to reach 300.

His best day came against Australia in Auckland in 1999–2000, when he took 7 for 87 on the way to 12 for 149 in the match. He led New Zealand in 32 Tests from 2007 to 2011, and in one-day cricket he played in the side that reached the 2015 World Cup final.

What made him special

He did not rip the ball. He beat batsmen with accuracy, flight and patience instead, and he was the first left-arm spinner to pass 300 wickets in both Tests and one-day internationals. He did all of it in glasses, which very few modern Test cricketers have tried.

His batting is a lovely story of late growth. His first 1,000 Test runs took him 47 matches, averaging 17.24. The next 1,000 needed only 22 Tests, at 42.52. His best score, 140, came against Sri Lanka in Colombo in August 2009, and he became the eighth man in Test history to reach 3,000 runs and 300 wickets.

Away from the middle

New Zealand honoured him in 2011, making him an Officer of its Order of Merit for his services to the game. He was also inducted into the New Zealand Cricket Hall of Fame. A biography, Turning Point, came out in 2008. His first cousin David Hill played a Test for the All Blacks.

Coaching followed. He led Royal Challengers Bangalore from 2014 to 2018, coached Bangladesh's spinners, became an assistant coach of Australia in May 2022, and took over at Sunrisers Hyderabad in August 2023.

And finally

He was one of the most recognisable figures in the game, and the glasses helped. Batsmen who saw him coming knew exactly who he was. Knowing what he was about to bowl was a different matter.
